title: Balanced Brackets With an ArrayDeque
statement:
`(`, `[` and `{` each need to be closed by the matching `)`, `]` or `}` --
and closed in the right order: `([)]` is not balanced even though it has
one of each character, because the `[` opens *after* the `(` but closes
*before* it does. A stack is built for exactly this shape of problem: the
most recently opened bracket is always the first one that has to close.

## Your function

```
public static boolean isBalanced(String text);
```

`text` may contain any characters; only `(`, `)`, `[`, `]`, `{` and `}`
participate in the check, and every other character is ignored. Return
`true` if every closing bracket matches the type of the most recently
unclosed opening bracket, and no opening bracket is left unclosed at the
end.

## Watch out

- **Use `Deque<Character>`, not `java.util.Stack`.** `Stack` still exists
  in Java, but it predates the collections framework, extends `Vector`,
  and carries synchronization overhead this single-threaded function gets
  no benefit from -- the standard library's own documentation recommends
  `Deque` (backed by `ArrayDeque`) instead. `Deque` provides `push`,
  `pop` and `peek` directly, with LIFO stack semantics, so switching costs
  nothing in how the code reads.
- **`pop()` and `peek()` on an empty `Deque` throw
  `NoSuchElementException`.** That is at least a well-defined, catchable
  exception rather than undefined behaviour -- but this function is asked
  to return `false` for an unmatched closing bracket, not let an exception
  propagate out of it. Check `.isEmpty()` *before* calling either one, for
  a closing bracket that arrives with nothing open to match it.
- **A stack that is not empty at the end means something was opened and
  never closed.** `"(()"` never sees a closing bracket it disagrees with
  -- every `)` it does see matches correctly -- so the mismatch can only
  be caught by checking the stack is empty once `text` is exhausted, not
  by anything that happens while consuming it.
